p: My name is Kuzey Aydın. I'm eleven, I live in Istanbul, and until last Saturday I thought the only strange thing about me was that the wind sometimes whispered to me.

Then a storm came, and my grandmother told me the truth. Our family belongs to a secret society called the Order of the Compass Rose. For nine hundred years, it has guarded seven bronze Keys, each holding the heart of one of the great winds. If anyone collects all seven and opens the Gate of Seven Winds, they will control the weather of the whole world.
And I'm a Windborn. The first in a hundred years. The winds talk to me, and sometimes, if I ask nicely, they help.

A man called Mordecai Vane wants the Keys. He has a hand made of gray stone, an army of fog-eyed men called the Grays, and twin children, Vex and Vera. He kidnapped my grandmother and took her to a gray tower by the sea.

With my cousin Ela and my best friend Bora, I fought a one-eyed giant in the Basilica Cistern, flew carpets in the Grand Bazaar, and found the first Key, the Yıldız, the North Wind. It lives inside me now. When I breathe out, my breath comes out frosty.
Grandma left me a letter. It said the next Key was in "the land where the winds were first given faces," in "the tower where eight brothers blow."
So now we're on a plane to Greece.
**Kuzey Aydın,** 11. A Windborn. Has the North Wind inside him. Still learning not to freeze his dinner.
**Ela Aydın,** 12. Kuzey's cousin. Keeper of the Clue Book. Has read a book about almost everything.
**Bora Kaya,** 11. Kuzey's best friend. Big, kind, brave, hungry. Has a cousin in every city. Possibly also in Greece.
**Uncle Tarık.** Ela's dad. Archaeologist. Gets very excited about old stones.
**Grandma Nermin.** The Keeper of the North Wind. Prisoner of Mordecai Vane.
**Mordecai Vane,** "the Gray Hand." Leader of the Ashen Circle. Wants all seven Keys.
**Vex Vane,** 13. Mordecai's son. Wears a gray glove like his father's.
**Vera Vane,** 13. Mordecai's daughter. Seems to be on her father's side. Seems to be.

chapters.t: Chapter One: Wind in My Pocket
p: Here is something nobody tells you about having the North Wind living inside you: it makes airplane food cold.

Every time I breathed on my tray, the rice froze. The chicken grew little white crystals. The orange juice turned into an orange ice lolly. The flight attendant on the plane to Athens looked at my frozen rice, then at me, then at the frost growing on my window in the shape of tiny ferns, and decided not to ask.

"You have to learn control," said Ela from the seat next to me. She had the Clue Book open on her tray table, covered in notes about Greek wind gods. "Yesterday you sneezed and blew the curtains off Dad's window."
"That was an accident."
"So was the ferry seagull."
The ferry seagull was a sensitive subject. Let's just say I sneezed again, on the ferry to Moda, and a seagull flew backwards for about a hundred meters with a very surprised face.

Across the aisle, Bora was eating his own dinner, then mine (he said frozen rice was "like a crunchy snack"), then the one the old lady next to him didn't want. She was Greek, and she was so happy to see a boy who loved food that she gave him half a bag of pistachios and pinched his cheek. Bora told her she was very kind. She didn't speak Turkish, and Bora doesn't speak Greek, but somehow they understood each other perfectly. Bora is like that.
Uncle Tarık sat in the row in front of us, snoring with his mouth open, a book called *Ancient Greek Weather Towers* on his face.
It had been two days since Grandma Nermin disappeared. Only two days. It felt like two years.
I still had her letter in my pocket. I had read it so many times that the paper had gone soft as cloth.
I reached into my jacket for it, and my fingers touched something else. A small folded paper I had never seen before. It was tucked deep into the inside pocket, behind Grandma's letter.
I opened it. The handwriting was neat, sharp and unfamiliar. Little straight letters, all leaning slightly forward, like they were in a hurry.
*He keeps her in a gray tower by the sea. She is alive. She is not hurt. I'm sorry. Please don't tell anyone I wrote this. — V*
I read it three times. Then I showed it to Ela.
She read it twice, and her eyebrows climbed so high they nearly reached her braids.
"V," she said. "Vex or Vera."

"Vera," I said. I remembered her on Galata Tower, holding her brother's arm. Giving me that little nod toward the stairs. And on the roof, watching our ferry leave, not calling anyone. "It has to be Vera."
"When did she put it in your pocket?"
I thought about it. "On the tower. When we pushed past them to get to the stairs. She was right next to me."

"So she wrote it *before* she came to the tower," Ela said slowly. "She planned it." She tapped her pencil against her teeth, which is what she does when she's thinking very hard. "Kuzey. Either Vera Vane wants to help us, or this is a trap. A very clever trap. Maybe her father told her to write it, so we'd trust her. So we'd lead them to the Keys."
"She looked sad," I said. "On the dock. And on the tower."
"Villains can look sad," said Ela. "In books, the sad-looking ones are the most dangerous."
"This isn't a book."
"Everything is a book," said Ela, "if you write it down."

I looked out the window at the clouds. The wind out there was talking, a thousand voices in a language I almost understood. Up here, so high, the winds were fast and cold and very busy, rushing around the world like people late for a train.
"Maybe," I said, "it's both. A trap and help. Maybe she doesn't know which side she's on."
Ela looked at me for a long moment. Then she wrote something in the Clue Book. I leaned over to see.
*Vera Vane: ??? Keep watching.*
Athens is hot even in November, full of orange trees, stray cats and ruins so old they make Istanbul's look like they were built last week.

We came out of the airport into bright sunshine, and the first thing I noticed was that the air smelled different. At home, the wind smells of the sea and simit and diesel from the ferries. Here it smelled of dust, thyme, oranges and something else, something old and warm, like the inside of an ancient library.
The second thing I noticed was that the winds were *loud.*

At home, the winds whisper. Here, they shouted. They argued. They interrupted each other. It was like walking into a café full of old men who have been arguing about football for a thousand years and are not going to stop just because a kid has arrived.
*Who's that?* *A boy. A boy with the North in him!* *Nonsense. Boreas would never live in a boy.* *Not Boreas, you old fool, the Turkish one, the Yıldız!* *Who are you calling an old fool?*
I put my hands over my ears. It didn't help. You can't put your hands over your ears to stop something that's inside your head.
"Kuzey?" Bora was looking at me with concern. "You've gone a funny color. Like yogurt."
"The winds," I said. "They're so loud here."
"What are they saying?"
"Mostly insulting each other."

Uncle Tarık had booked us two rooms in a little hotel in Plaka, the oldest neighborhood in Athens, right under the Acropolis. The streets there are narrow and twisty, full of white houses with blue shutters, bright pink flowers spilling over walls, and little shops selling sponges, olive oil soap and plastic statues of Greek gods. Cats sleep on every step, every car roof and every windowsill. Bora tried to count them and gave up at sixty-three.

The hotel was run by an old Greek lady called Kyria Despina, who wore black and had a mustache and fed us so much that even Bora was impressed. She brought us moussaka, which is like a lasagna made with eggplant, and tiny fried cheese pies, and a salad with a slab of white cheese on top as big as a book, and a honey cake soaked in syrup.
"I love Greece," said Bora, with his mouth full. "Greece is my favorite country. Sorry, Turkey."
"Turkey also has börek," Ela pointed out.
"Turkey is also my favorite country," said Bora. "I can have two."
After dinner, Uncle Tarık went to call a friend from the university, and the three of us climbed up to the hotel's tiny roof terrace.
The sun had set. And above us, so close that it felt like you could reach out and touch it, was the Acropolis.

It's a huge flat-topped rock that rises out of the middle of the city, with steep cliffs all around. On the top, lit up gold against the dark blue sky, stands the Parthenon: a great temple of white marble columns, built two and a half thousand years ago for the goddess Athena. It looks like it's floating above the city. Like a crown made of light.
We just stood there and looked at it.
"Two and a half thousand years," whispered Ela. "People stood right here and looked at it two and a half thousand years ago. Just like us."
The winds of Athens had gone quiet. Even they were looking.
Then, very softly, one of them spoke. Not shouting this time. A warm, gentle voice, smelling of the sea.
*You came at last, little brother. Tomorrow, come to the tower. We have been waiting a long time. Come when the sun is past the middle of the sky. I will show you.*
"Who are you?" I whispered.
But the voice was gone.
I didn't sleep much that night. Partly because Bora snores like a motorbike. Partly because I was thinking about Vera's note. And partly because, at two in the morning, I sneezed.
I had a little cold from the airplane. My nose had been tickling all evening. And at two in the morning, it finally exploded.
"A-a-a-CHOO!"

The window blew open. The curtains flew straight out sideways like flags. Every piece of paper in the room took off and swirled around the ceiling, including Ela's notes, which she had left on the table. The lamp fell over. And a thin layer of frost covered absolutely everything, including Bora, who woke up with a little white crust on his eyebrows.
"Wha?" he said. "Is it snowing? Are we in Iceland?"
"No," I said miserably. "It's me."
Ela came in from the next room in her pajamas, with her glasses on crooked and a flashlight. She looked at the papers swirling around the ceiling. She looked at the frost. She looked at me.
"Right," she said. "That's it. Tomorrow morning, training."
Ela takes training very seriously.

At six o'clock, before breakfast, she marched us up to the roof terrace. She had a list. Of course she had a list. It was titled *KUZEY WIND CONTROL TRAINING PROGRAM (DRAFT)* and it had eleven points.
"Point one," she said. "Breathing. You froze everything because you breathed out too hard. A Windborn needs to control his breath. Like a singer. Or a trumpet player. Or a dragon."
"Dragons don't control their breath," said Bora. "That's the whole point of dragons."
"*Good* dragons do," said Ela firmly.
She put a candle on the table and lit it. "Breathe on the candle," she said. "Gently. Make the flame lean over. But don't blow it out, and don't freeze it."
I breathed on the candle.
It froze. The whole candle, flame and all. The flame turned into a little yellow ice crystal, standing on top of a candle covered in frost.
"Huh," said Ela. She wrote something down. "That's... actually amazing. But no."

I tried again. And again. And again. By the tenth try, I could make the flame lean over without freezing it. By the twentieth, I could make it lean left and then right, like it was dancing. Bora clapped.
"Point two," said Ela. "Distance."
She put a paper cup on the wall at the other end of the terrace. "Knock it over. Just the cup. Nothing else."
The first time, I knocked over the cup, the wall, a flowerpot, and a cat that had been sleeping on the wall, who landed on her feet on the roof next door and gave me a look of pure hatred.
The tenth time, I knocked over just the cup.
"Point three," said Ela. "Asking. You said on Bora's roof that the wind doesn't like being told what to do. So practice asking. Ask the wind to bring us something."
I closed my eyes. I listened to the morning winds of Athens. They were quieter now, still sleepy, yawning over the rooftops.
"Excuse me," I said politely. "Good morning. Could someone please bring me something nice?"
There was a long pause. Then a little breeze came over the wall, carrying something. It dropped it gently on the table in front of me.
It was a fresh, warm, sesame-covered bread ring, like a simit. In Greece, they're called koulouri.
A second later, from the street below, we heard a man shouting angrily in Greek. A koulouri seller, with his tray on his head, looking around in every direction for his missing bread.
"Oh no," I said.
Bora ran down the stairs to pay him. When he came back, he had bought six more.
Ela wrote in her list: *Point 3: Partly successful. Wind needs to learn about stealing.*

chapters.t: Chapter Four: The Gods of the Air
p: After breakfast (koulouri, yogurt with honey, more moussaka, which Kyria Despina insisted was a breakfast food), Uncle Tarık took us to the Acropolis.
"We don't need to go to the tower until the afternoon," he said. "The wind said after the middle of the day. And you cannot come to Athens and not see the Parthenon. It's against the law."
"Is it really?" asked Bora.
"It should be," said Uncle Tarık.

We climbed up the steep path, between olive trees and old stones, with hundreds of other tourists from every country in the world. At the top, we walked through a huge gateway of marble columns, and there it was. The Parthenon, up close.

It was bigger than I expected. Much bigger. The columns were as thick as tree trunks and as tall as houses. Some of them were broken, and there was scaffolding on one side, where workers were fixing it. But it was still the most beautiful building I had ever seen. The marble glowed honey-gold in the morning sun.
Uncle Tarık was so happy that he kept stopping in the middle of the path to explain things, and people kept walking into him.

"Notice," he said, "that the columns are not straight! They lean in, very slightly, and they're a tiny bit fatter in the middle. The Greeks did this on purpose, so that from far away, they would *look* straight! Isn't that wonderful?"
"Wonderful," said Bora, who was looking at a man selling ice cream at the bottom of the hill.
But I was looking at the sky.
Up here, on top of the rock, the winds were wild. They came from every direction, whipping around the columns, tugging at people's hats and maps. And they were talking about me. I could hear them.
*That's him.* *So small!* *He tamed the koulouri wind this morning.* *Tamed? He asked it nicely. There's a difference.*
"Uncle Tarık," I said. "Did the Greeks have a god of the wind?"
Uncle Tarık's eyes lit up like I had given him a birthday present.

"Not one! Many!" He sat down on a block of marble and waved his arms. "The king of the winds was called Aeolus. He lived on a floating island, and he kept all the winds locked up in a cave, letting them out one at a time. In the *Odyssey,* the great old story, the hero Odysseus is trying to sail home from the war. Aeolus wants to help him, so he gives Odysseus a leather bag with all the bad winds tied up inside it. 'Don't open it,' he says. Only the gentle west wind is left outside, to blow Odysseus's ship home."
"What happened?" asked Ela, writing it down.

"They sailed for nine days. They could see their home island. They could see the smoke from the houses! And Odysseus fell asleep. And his sailors thought the bag must be full of gold. So they opened it." Uncle Tarık threw his hands up. "WHOOSH! All the winds came out at once, in a terrible storm, and blew them all the way back to where they started."
"That's so sad," said Bora.
"It's a lesson," said Uncle Tarık. "The winds are not treasure. You can't keep them in a bag. Not for long."
I thought of Mordecai's gray hand. Of Vex's glove. Of the Lodos Key, waiting somewhere, and the Gate of Seven Winds.
*Not for long,* whispered a wind around the columns of the Parthenon. *Remember that, little brother.*

"And then there were the four big winds," Uncle Tarık went on. "The Anemoi. Boreas, the north wind, who was cold and stormy and had a purple beard. Notos, the south wind, who brought the rain at the end of summer. Euros, the east wind, who was unlucky. And Zephyros, the west wind, the gentlest of them all, who brought the spring flowers."
"The west wind," said Ela suddenly. "Grandma said the west wind is the one that wouldn't make a deal. In the Order."

Uncle Tarık looked surprised. "Did she? How interesting. Zephyros was always the free one. The one who blew wherever he liked." He stood up and brushed the marble dust off his trousers. "Well. Shall we go and meet the other four?"

The Tower of the Winds stands in the Roman Agora, near the bottom of the Acropolis hill. The Agora was once a great market, where people bought and sold olive oil and wine and argued about philosophy. Now it's a big field of broken columns, old walls and wild grass, with cats sleeping everywhere and lizards running over the warm stones.
And in the middle of it stands the tower.

It's a strange little building, tall and white, with eight sides, each one facing a different direction. Two thousand years ago it was a clock, a weather vane and a calendar all at once. There was a bronze statue of a sea god on top that turned with the wind. Inside was a water clock, powered by a stream from the Acropolis. And on the outside, under each wind god, were sundials that told the time.
"It's the oldest weather station in the world," said Uncle Tarık, his voice full of love. "A man called Andronikos built it. Look up. Near the top of each side."
I looked up.

Near the top of each of the eight walls was a carving of a flying man. Each one was different. Some were old with beards, some were young. Some wore thick cloaks, some wore almost nothing. They floated sideways across the marble, their robes streaming behind them, as if the wind they were made of was blowing them along.

"Boreas, the north wind, with his conch shell," said Uncle Tarık happily, pointing with his umbrella. He was in his element. "Look at his thick cloak, because the north wind is cold. Kaikias, the northeast, dropping hail from a shield. Apeliotes, the east, carrying fruit and grain, because he brings the gentle rain. Euros, the southeast, wrapped up in his cloak because he's grumpy. Notos, the south, pouring rain from a jar. Lips..."
"Lips?" said Bora. "There's a god called *Lips?*"
"The southwest wind," said Ela, flipping pages. "In Turkish, that's Lodos. Look, he's holding the back of a ship. Because the southwest wind pushes ships into the harbor."
"Zephyros, the west wind, with his lap full of flowers," Uncle Tarık went on. "And Skiron, the northwest, tipping out a pot of hot ashes."
"Eight brothers," I said. "The tower where eight brothers blow."
It was past the middle of the day. The sun was sliding toward the west. The shadows of the old columns were getting longer across the grass.
I walked slowly around the tower. Past cold Boreas. Past grumpy Euros. Past Zephyros and his flowers. And I stopped under Lips, the southwest wind, the one holding the ship.
I closed my eyes.
The winds of Athens all started talking at once.

*Windborn! A Windborn, here, after so long!* *He is small.* *He is Turkish, the north speaks through him, I can smell the Bosphorus.* *He has a cold. Listen to him sniff.* *QUIET, all of you,* said a warm, deep voice, and they went quiet. *Let the boy ask.*
It was the same voice from the roof terrace. The one smelling of the sea.
"Lips," I whispered. "Is that you?"
*It is, little brother.*
"Please. Where is the Lodos Key?"

The warm wind stroked my face like a hand. *My Turkish cousin, the Lodos, sleeps far from here, across the sea. I cannot carry you there. But I can show you the way. Look at my shadow, little brother. The sun still tells the time on my wall.*
I opened my eyes.

Under each wind god, there were thin lines carved into the marble, spreading out like the spokes of a fan. Sundials. A small bronze rod stuck out from the wall above them, and its shadow fell across the lines, telling the time.

The afternoon sun cast the rod's shadow on the sundial under Lips. And where the shadow touched the stone, just at the tip of it, some letters seemed to glow faintly. Pale gold, like sunlight on water. Letters you could only see at that exact moment, at that exact time, on that exact wall.
"Ela!" I said. "Look!"
Ela was already copying them. "They're Greek," she said. "Ancient Greek. Dad, can you read them? Quick, before the shadow moves!"
Uncle Tarık squinted at the wall. He took off his glasses, cleaned them on his shirt, put them back on and squinted again. His lips moved as he read. And his face went pale under his beard.
"'Where the bronze guardian walked the shore three times a day,'" he read slowly, "'the warm wind sleeps in the house of the bull.'"
The shadow moved on. The letters faded, and were gone.
§CLUE Where the bronze guardian walked the shore three times a day, the warm wind sleeps in the house of the bull.

"Bronze guardian," said Ela, eyes shining. "Talos! In the myths, Talos was a giant made of bronze, made by the god of fire. He walked around the whole island of Crete three times every day to protect it from pirates. He threw rocks at ships. And the house of the bull..."
"The Minotaur," I said. I knew that story. Everybody does. Half man, half bull, living in the middle of a maze. "The labyrinth. On Crete."
"Knossos!" said Ela and Uncle Tarık together.
"Correct," said a voice behind us. "Ten points for the Turkish children."
Vex Vane sat on a broken column, eating a pistachio ice cream.

He was wearing sunglasses and a white shirt, like a tourist, and he looked completely relaxed, swinging his legs. But his gray glove was on his right hand, and the ice cream in his left hand was frozen solid. He was biting it, not licking it.

Behind him stood six tall men in identical gray suits and gray sunglasses, their faces strangely blank, like mannequins in a shop window. Nobody else in the Agora seemed to notice them. The tourists walked right past, taking photos of the tower, as if the gray men were part of the ruins.
"Meet the Grays," said Vex, crunching his ice cream. "Father's employees. They don't talk much. They also don't feel pain, which is useful."
Vera stood a little apart from her brother. She was wearing a big straw hat, and she didn't look at me.
"Kids," said Uncle Tarık nervously, "do you know these people?"
"That's the guy whose dad kidnapped Grandma," Bora said.

Uncle Tarık stood up very straight. He was not a big man. He was not a strong man. He had never been in a fight in his life, as far as I knew, except possibly an argument about Roman pottery. But he lifted his umbrella like a sword and stepped in front of us.
"Young man," he said to Vex, in his best university voice, "I am an archaeologist, and I am not afraid of you."
"Great," said Vex. "Grays, take the needle from the boy."
"There is no needle," I said quickly. "I don't have it. It's gone."

Vex laughed. "I know. It's inside you. Father told me. That's okay. You'll do even better." He finished his ice cream and stood up. "Father wants *you,* Windborn. He wants you to come with us and find the rest of the Keys for him. Nicely. Without any fuss. And then maybe your grandmother can go home." He smiled. "See? Easy."
"No," I said.
"I thought you might say that." He snapped his gloved fingers. "Grays."
The Grays moved forward all together, smooth as robots.

I didn't think. I just breathed in, and felt the cold of the North Wind fill my chest like a balloon, and I remembered Ela's training. *Breathe like a singer. Like a trumpet player. Like a good dragon.*
And I *blew.*

A blast of icy wind shot out of my mouth. Not a wild explosion this time, but a narrow, straight jet of cold, like water from a hose. It hit the first two Grays right in the chest and knocked them flat on their backs on the ancient stones. Their sunglasses flew off.
Underneath, their eyes were completely gray. No pupils. No color. Like fog in a jar.
"Okay," said Bora. "That's creepy. That's the creepiest thing I've ever seen, and I've seen Tepegöz."
The two Grays sat up. They didn't look hurt. They didn't look angry. They didn't look anything. They just got up, put their sunglasses back on, and kept coming.
The other four were coming too.
Uncle Tarık bonked one on the head with his umbrella. The Gray didn't even blink. The umbrella bent in half. Uncle Tarık looked at it sadly. "That was a good umbrella," he said.

Ela threw the Clue Book at another one, and immediately regretted it, and ran to get the Clue Book back from under the Gray's feet. Bora grabbed her by the collar and pulled her away just as gray fingers reached for her.
Cold mist was rising from the Grays now. Frost was spreading across the grass. A lizard on a stone froze in the middle of a step.
And the winds of Athens were laughing in my head.
*Little brother needs help!* *Look at the gray ones! No color in them at all! Disgusting!* *Shall we?* *Shall we, little brother? Just ask!*
"Yes, please!" I shouted out loud. "All of you! Please!"
Eight winds at once came whirling down from the Tower.

North and south, east and west and everything in between. Cold Boreas and warm Notos, gentle Zephyros and grumpy Euros, all of them, all together, for the first time in who knows how many hundreds of years. They came down from the eight walls of the tower like the stone carvings had come to life, and they hit the Agora in a roaring, spinning, laughing circle.

Dust exploded off the ancient stones. Leaves, paper cups, tourist maps, hats, a postcard rack, a very surprised cat and every single pigeon in the Agora flew up into the air in a great roaring spiral, round and round the tower. The Grays stumbled and spun like tops. One of them was lifted right off his feet and spun around in midair three times before landing in a bush.
Vex grabbed onto a column and held on, his white shirt flapping, his sunglasses gone. "STOP IT!" he yelled. "STOP IT!"
Tourists were screaming and running. A tour guide was shouting at everyone to stay calm, while her umbrella flew away over her head like a little colored bird.
"RUN!" I shouted.

We ran. Out of the Agora, through a gap in the fence, down a street of souvenir shops where the wind was knocking over racks of postcards and plastic Parthenons. Past a man selling grilled corn from a cart. Bora grabbed one without stopping. (He went back and paid later. He promised.)
But the Grays were already behind us. They had climbed out of the bushes and up off the ground, and now they were following, walking fast, all six of them, in step, the way they always did.
"They don't get tired," panted Ela. "Remember what Rıza Usta said! They never get tired!"
"Well, *I* get tired!" puffed Bora, eating his corn as he ran.

We turned into the twisty streets of Plaka. Up stairs, down alleys, under arches covered in flowers. The streets were so narrow that the houses almost touched over our heads. Cats leaped out of our way. An old man playing backgammon in a doorway shouted something in Greek.
Every time we turned a corner, the Grays were still there. Twenty meters behind. Then fifteen. Then ten.
"Kuzey!" shouted Ela. "Do something!"
I looked up. The narrow street was hung with washing lines between the houses, across the street from window to window, full of sheets and shirts and towels, drying in the sun.
I had done this before. In Istanbul. With the carpets.
"Wind," I said. I was running, gasping, and I could barely get the words out. "Please. The washing. The sheets."
*Ha! Like the carpets! We heard about the carpets!* said a breeze, delighted. Even the winds in Athens had heard. Winds love gossip.

It swept down the street behind us. Every sheet on every washing line flew off at once. White sheets, flowered sheets, a huge blue one with a picture of a footballer on it. They swooped down on the Grays like enormous ghosts and wrapped themselves around their heads.
Six gray men, completely covered in bedsheets, crashed into each other in the middle of the street, tripped over a cat, and fell over in a big flapping heap.
We ran out of the bottom of the street into a busy road, waving our arms. A yellow taxi screeched to a stop.
"The port of Piraeus!" Uncle Tarık gasped to the driver as we fell inside. "As fast as you can! We need the night ferry to Crete!"
The driver, a huge man with a mustache, looked at us in his mirror. Four sweaty people, covered in dust and leaves, one of them eating corn.
He shrugged, turned up his music, and drove like a rocket.

As the taxi pulled away, I looked back through the dust. Back down the street, a pile of bedsheets was struggling on the ground. And standing above it, alone, her straw hat gone, her pale hair blowing in the last of the wind, was Vera.
She was watching our taxi disappear.
She raised one hand. A tiny wave.
Then Vex came running around the corner behind her, furious, his shirt torn. He grabbed her arm and pulled her away.

The port of Piraeus is enormous. It's the biggest port in Greece, with dozens of ferries lined up along the docks like giant white whales, their back doors wide open, swallowing cars and trucks and buses and people. Horns blasted. Engines roared. Men in orange vests waved their arms and shouted. Seagulls screamed overhead.
Our taxi driver dropped us at the gate, turned his music up even louder, and roared away.
"Right," said Uncle Tarık, looking at the tickets on his phone. "Gate E2. The ship to Heraklion. It leaves at nine o'clock. We have forty minutes."
We hurried along the dock toward the huge blue-and-white ship.
And stopped.
At the bottom of the ramp, where the passengers were climbing aboard, stood two Grays. Checking every face. And at the top of the car ramp, where the trucks drove in, stood two more.
"How did they get here before us?" whispered Ela.
"They don't stop at traffic lights," said Bora darkly. "I bet they don't stop at anything."
We hid behind a stack of shipping containers and peered around the edge. The Grays hadn't seen us. Yet. But there was no way to get onto the ship without walking straight past them.
"There's another ferry tomorrow," said Uncle Tarık.
"Vex will be on Crete by tomorrow," said Ela. "He'll get to Knossos first."
We stood there, thinking. The ship's horn gave a long, low blast. *Thirty minutes.*
That was when a voice behind us shouted, "BORA?"
We spun around.

A young man was standing by a big truck loaded with crates of oranges. He was tall and round and cheerful, with curly black hair, a black beard and an orange vest, and he was staring at Bora with his mouth open.
"BORA KAYA?" he shouted again. "Little Bora? Aunt Ayşe's Bora?"
Bora's face split into a huge grin. "NIKOS!"
They ran at each other and hugged so hard that I heard something crack. (It was a crate of oranges that they had bumped into. Oranges rolled everywhere.)
"Your cousin?" said Ela faintly. "*Here?* In *Greece?*"

"My mom's cousin's son," said Bora happily. "His mom married a Greek man from the island of Lesbos. They came to my birthday when I was seven. Nikos taught me to juggle!" He turned to Nikos. "What are you doing here?"
"I drive this truck," said Nikos proudly. "Oranges to Crete. Every week. What are *you* doing here?"

Bora looked at us. We looked at Bora. Then Bora looked at Nikos, and he said, very seriously, "Nikos. We need to get on that ship without anyone seeing us. It's very important. There are some men in gray suits who want to stop us. They're bad men. I can't tell you why. But it's important."
Nikos looked at Bora. He looked at the Grays at the ramp. He looked at the three of us, and at Uncle Tarık in his dusty jacket, holding his bent umbrella.
"Bad men in gray suits," Nikos said slowly.
"Very bad," said Bora.
Nikos was quiet for a moment. Then he grinned, the same big grin as Bora's. You could tell they were related.
"Family is family," he said. "Get in the back."
The back of the truck was dark, and cold, and full of oranges.

Crates and crates of them, stacked to the ceiling, smelling so strongly of oranges that it made my eyes water. Nikos moved some of the crates to make a little cave in the middle, and the four of us squeezed inside. Then he put the crates back, all around us, so that from outside you couldn't see anything but oranges.
"Don't move," he whispered. "Don't sneeze. Don't eat the oranges."
Bora looked deeply hurt by the last one.

The doors slammed. The engine started. The truck rumbled forward and stopped. Forward and stopped. We were in the line for the ship. Through a crack between two crates, I could see a little slice of the outside: the dock, the lights, the big open mouth of the ship.
And a Gray.
He was standing right next to the truck. His foggy eyes were moving slowly over everything. He put his gray hand on the side of the truck.
Frost spread across the metal. I could hear it crackle. Through the crack, I saw a thin line of white creeping inside, across the floor, toward our crates.
Nobody breathed.
Then I heard Nikos's voice, loud and cheerful, from the driver's window.
"Hey! Hey, you! Friend! You want an orange? Best oranges in Greece! From Argos! Very sweet! Here, here, take two!"
The Gray turned his head slowly toward the window.
"Take them, take them! For your health! You look a bit gray, my friend! Very pale! You need vitamin C!"
There was a long pause.

Then the truck moved forward. The Gray had stepped back. Through the crack, I saw him standing on the dock, holding two oranges in his gray hands, staring at them with his blank fog eyes, as if he had never seen an orange before in his life and had no idea what to do with one.
The truck rumbled up the ramp, into the belly of the ship, and stopped.
The doors opened. Nikos's grinning face appeared between the crates.
"Welcome to the ship," he said. "Next stop, Crete."
Bora climbed out first and hugged him again, and this time he didn't knock over any oranges. Well, only a few.
"Nikos," he said. "You're the best cousin in the whole world."
"I know," said Nikos. He handed Bora an orange. "Now you can eat one."

The ferry to Crete leaves Piraeus every night at nine o'clock and arrives in the morning. It's a giant ship, as big as an apartment building, painted white and blue, with trucks and cars and buses driving into its open mouth at the back, and hundreds of people climbing aboard with suitcases, backpacks, boxes of vegetables, a goat. (Really. A man had a goat on a lead. Bora went to say hello to it.)

The night ferry smelled like diesel and fried cheese. We hadn't booked a cabin. Uncle Tarık had spent all his cash on the tickets and the taxi. So once Nikos had smuggled us up the stairs from the car deck, we slept in the big lounge, in airplane-style chairs, with about two hundred other people, a TV showing a Greek game show, and a man snoring so loudly that Bora said he was "impressed, professionally."
Bora, it turned out, gets seasick.

He found out about an hour after we left the harbor, when the ferry came out into the open sea and started to roll. Up, and down. Up, and down. Up, and down. Bora went from his normal color to white, then to a sort of pale green, like pistachio ice cream.
"I'm fine," he said, holding onto the arms of his chair. "I'm totally fine. Kuzey. Kuzey, can you make the sea stop moving?"
"I can't control the sea, Bora. Only wind."
"The wind makes the waves, though," said Ela, not looking up from the Clue Book. "Technically."
I looked at Bora's green face. Then I went out onto the deck.

It was dark and cold outside, and the wind was strong, blowing across the black sea, pushing up waves with white tops. The stars were out, millions of them, more than I had ever seen in Istanbul. The ferry's lights made a long golden road on the water behind us.
"Hello," I said to the wind. "Sorry to bother you. My friend feels sick. Could you... maybe blow a bit more gently? Just for tonight?"
The wind of the open sea was different from all the winds I had met before. It was huge and slow and very, very calm, like a whale. It thought about my question for a long time.
*For you, small one,* it said at last, in a voice as deep as the ocean. *For one night.*
It softened. The waves went down. The ferry stopped rolling and slid smoothly over the water, like a skater on ice.
When I came back inside, Bora was asleep, snoring, and his face was its normal color again.
Ela wasn't asleep. Of course she wasn't.

She was sitting on the floor by the window, the Clue Book open on her knees, a flashlight in her mouth, going through the photos of Knossos that she had downloaded at the hotel. When she saw me, she took the flashlight out of her mouth.
"Can't sleep?"
"No."
I sat down next to her. Out the window, the dark sea slid by.
"I keep thinking about Vera," I said. "She waved. Why would she wave?"
Ela was quiet for a moment.

"I've been thinking about her too," she said. "Here's what I know. One: she stopped her brother at Galata Tower. Two: she told us to run. Three: she watched our ferry leave and didn't tell anyone. Four: she wrote you a note saying your grandmother is alive. Five: today, she didn't try to stop us at all. She just watched." She tapped her pencil on the page. "That's a lot of evidence."
"Evidence of what?"

"That she doesn't want to be doing this." Ela pushed up her glasses. "But that doesn't mean she'll help us, Kuzey. She's still his daughter. When it really matters, she might choose him. People usually choose their family."
I thought about that. About Grandma. About my parents on the ice. About Uncle Tarık holding up his umbrella against six Grays.
"Yeah," I said. "I would too."
Ela closed the Clue Book and leaned her head on my shoulder. A minute later, she was asleep.

I stayed awake until the sky started to turn gray in the east. And just before dawn, out in the dark water beside the ferry, I saw them. Dolphins. Five of them, jumping and racing alongside the ship, silver in the first light, leaping in and out of the waves as if they were laughing.
I didn't wake anyone. I just watched them. And for a little while, I wasn't worried about anything at all.

chapters.t: Chapter Ten: Meanwhile, in a Hotel in Athens
p: *This is another part of the story that Kuzey didn't see. Someone told him about it, much later.*
Vex Vane sat on the edge of the bath in a very expensive hotel room in Athens, with his gray glove off, holding his right hand under the cold tap.

It hurt. It always hurt, after he used the glove. Like holding a snowball for too long. His fingers were red and stiff, and there were little gray marks on his fingertips, like ink stains that wouldn't wash off.
They had been there for two months now. They were getting bigger.
He didn't tell anyone. Not his father. Not even Vera.
From the other room came the sound of a phone ringing. Then his father's voice, cold and smooth, through the speaker.
"Vex."
Vex turned off the tap and dried his hand quickly. He went into the room and stood very straight in front of the phone, as if his father could see him.
"Yes, Father."
"You lost them."
"They had help. The winds of Athens. All eight of them. There was nothing I could..."
"There is always something you can do." A pause. The phone crackled with cold. "Where are they going?"
"Crete. Knossos. We followed them to the port. They're on the night ferry."

"Then follow them. Take the Grays. Get there before them, if you can. And Vex." His father's voice went even colder. "I don't need the boy to love me. I don't need him to come willingly. I need him to *find things.* So let him find the Key. And then take it from him. Do you understand?"
"Yes, Father."
"Good. Don't disappoint me again."
The phone went dead.
Vex stood there for a long time, looking at it.
Behind him, the door to the other bedroom opened. Vera stood there in her pajamas.
"You don't have to do everything he says," she said quietly.
"Yes, I do," said Vex. He didn't turn around. "That's what we're for. That's what *you're* for too. Or did you forget?"
"I didn't forget."
"Then why didn't you help me today?" He spun around. His face was red. "Why did you just stand there? You saw what they did to me! The sheets! Everyone was laughing!"
Vera looked at her brother. At his red face. At his right hand, which he was holding behind his back.
"Show me your hand," she said.
"No."
"Vex. Show me your hand."
He hesitated. Then, slowly, he brought it out.

Vera looked at the little gray marks on his fingertips for a long time. She didn't say anything. She took his hand in both of hers and held it, the way their mother used to, a long time ago, when they were small and had bad dreams.
Vex let her. Just for a minute.
Then he pulled his hand away, and went to bed, and didn't say good night.
By morning, Crete rose out of the sea.

It's the biggest island in Greece, long and narrow, with green hills, white villages, olive trees by the million, and far in the distance, a line of high mountains with snow on their tops. As the ferry came into the harbor of Heraklion, the sun was rising behind the mountains, turning the snow pink.

Bora woke up and announced that he was "starving, completely, like never before in history." We had breakfast in a café by the harbor, next to an old Venetian fortress with a stone lion carved on its wall. Crete has bread with olives, cheese pies with honey, and a kind of thick yogurt that Bora said he wanted to marry.
Then Uncle Tarık insisted on going to the museum.
"We need to understand the Minoans," he said. "The people who built Knossos. If we're going into their palace, we need to understand how they *thought.*"
Ela agreed. Bora said he would agree to anything if there was a café in the museum. There was.

The Heraklion Archaeological Museum is full of things from four thousand years ago, and none of them look the way you'd expect ancient things to look. The Minoans loved color. Their walls were covered in paintings of blue monkeys, leaping dolphins, flowers, birds, and women with curly hair and huge sleeves. They made cups shaped like bull heads, with gold horns. They made tiny statues of goddesses holding snakes in each hand.
"Snakes again," said Bora. "Why is it always snakes?"
And in one room, there was a painting that stopped all three of us.

It showed a huge charging bull, white with brown patches, its head down, its horns sharp. And three young people were *leaping over it.* One was grabbing the bull's horns. One was doing a backflip over its back. One was landing behind it with her arms out, like a gymnast.
"Bull-leaping," said Uncle Tarık softly. "The Minoans did it for sport. Or maybe for religion. Nobody is quite sure. They'd run straight at a charging bull, grab its horns, and flip over it."
"That's crazy," said Bora, with deep admiration.
"That's brave," said Ela.
"That's the house of the bull," I said.
They looked at me.

"The clue," I said. "The warm wind sleeps in the house of the bull. Everyone thinks it means the Minotaur. But the Minoans loved bulls. Everything in their palace was about bulls. Maybe 'the house of the bull' just means the palace. Their palace."
"Which is Knossos," said Ela. "So we were right anyway."
"I know," I said. "But I think it means we have to look for bulls. Not just a maze."
Ela looked at me. Then she grinned and wrote it down.

In the next room, there was a glass case with a single object in it. A double-headed axe, made of gold, so thin and delicate that you could never have chopped anything with it. Its two blades curved out on either side like the wings of a butterfly.

"The labrys," said Uncle Tarık. "The sacred double axe of the Minoans. It was their most holy symbol. It's carved all over Knossos. Some people think the word *labyrinth* comes from it. 'The house of the double axe.'"
I looked at it for a long time. The two blades. The handle in the middle.
There was a tiny shape engraved on the handle, so small that I had to put my nose against the glass to see it.
A compass rose. With seven points.

chapters.t: Chapter Twelve: The Storm at Büyükada
p: That evening, after the museum, we sat on the old harbor wall in Heraklion, eating grilled octopus (Bora), a cheese pie (Ela), nothing (me) and three cups of coffee (Uncle Tarık). The fishing boats bobbed in the water. The lights of the Venetian fortress were coming on at the end of the harbor wall, yellow against the purple sky.
Uncle Tarık was quiet. That's unusual. Normally Uncle Tarık talks the way other people breathe.
"Dad?" said Ela. "Are you okay?"
"I was thinking about your grandmother," he said. "About a day, a long time ago. I didn't understand it then. I think I understand it now."
He put down his coffee.

"When I was ten, and your mother was eight," he said to me, "Mum took us sailing. Just the three of us. In a little wooden boat she borrowed from a fisherman, off the island of Büyükada, in the Sea of Marmara. It was a beautiful summer day. Blue sky. Calm sea. We had sandwiches and lemonade."
"What happened?" said Bora, with his mouth full of octopus.

"A storm came," said Uncle Tarık. "Out of nowhere. Out of a completely blue sky. Black clouds, from the south. Lodos. The sea went crazy. Waves taller than the boat. The sail ripped. Your mother was screaming. I was screaming. We were both sure we were going to drown."
He looked out at the dark sea.

"And Mum stood up," he said. "In the middle of the boat, in the storm, with the waves crashing over us. She stood up, and she held onto the mast, and she started to sing. That old Black Sea song. The one about the fisherman."
I felt the hair on my arms stand up.

"And the storm stopped," said Uncle Tarık quietly. "Not all at once. But the wind went down, and the waves went down, and the black clouds just... drifted apart. In about two minutes, it was sunny again. Mum sat down and handed us each a sandwich, and said, 'Well, that was exciting, wasn't it?' And that was it. We never talked about it again."
"She wasn't a Windborn," said Ela slowly. "Grandma said she wasn't. Only Kuzey and Kaptan Murat."

"No," said Uncle Tarık. "I don't think she could command the wind. I think she just... asked it. Very nicely. And it liked her so much that it listened." He smiled sadly. "For forty years I told myself it was a coincidence. Storms stop all the time. I'm a scientist. I believe in evidence."
He looked at me.
"And then I came down the stairs under the Serpent Column, and my nephew breathed out snow."
Nobody said anything for a while. The waves lapped against the harbor wall.

"Kuzey," said Uncle Tarık. "I'm not brave like your grandmother. I can't talk to the wind. I'm not clever like Ela, or strong like Bora. I'm just a man who knows a lot about old pots." He took off his glasses and rubbed his eyes. "But I promise you, I will do everything I can to get her back. Everything."
"You stood in front of six Grays with an umbrella," I said.
"It bent," said Uncle Tarık.
"You still stood there," said Ela, and she leaned against her father's shoulder.
Uncle Tarık put his arm around her, and then, after a moment, around me too. Bora wiped his eyes on his sleeve and pretended it was the onions.

chapters.t: Chapter Thirteen: The House of the Bull
p: The palace of Knossos is almost four thousand years old.

It was the center of the Minoan world, a giant building with more than a thousand rooms, spread over a hill among olive trees and cypress trees, five kilometers from the sea. There were kings and queens there, priests and priestesses, workshops, storerooms full of giant clay jars of oil and wine, bathrooms with real flushing toilets (Bora was very interested in this), and grand staircases going up and down between floors.

It's mostly ruins now. A maze of low walls, broken stairs going nowhere, courtyards full of tourists, and a few rooms that someone rebuilt a hundred years ago, with bright red columns that get thinner at the bottom instead of the top, like upside-down tree trunks.

"It was so big and so confusing," said Uncle Tarık, "that the Greeks who came later thought it *was* the Labyrinth. The home of the Minotaur. They saw all these rooms and corridors and stairs, and they thought, 'Nobody could ever find their way out of here.'"
"I believe them," said Bora. "I'm lost already, and we've only been here five minutes."

It was hot. The sun beat down on the old stones. Cicadas were singing in the trees, a loud dry buzzing sound like a thousand tiny electric razors. There were tourists everywhere: tour groups following guides with flags, families with strollers, couples taking selfies in front of the red columns.
And no Grays. I checked. I checked very carefully.
"Okay," said Ela. She had the Clue Book in one hand and a map of Knossos in the other. "So where do we start? This place has a thousand rooms."
I closed my eyes and listened.

The wind at Knossos was warm and lazy. It came up from the sea, through the olive trees, and drifted around the ruins very slowly, like a cat walking around a sunny garden, stopping to sniff things. It didn't want to talk. It was too hot to talk.
*Mmm,* it said, when I asked it where the Lodos Key was. *Sleeping. Everything sleeps here. Too hot. Go away.*
"It's not helping," I said.
"Then we do it the old-fashioned way," said Ela. "With our brains." She pointed. "There."
Carved into a big stone block near the entrance was a symbol. Two triangles joined at the points, with a line through the middle. An axe with two blades, like a butterfly.

"The labrys," she said. "The double axe. Like the gold one in the museum. With the tiny compass rose on it." She flipped through her photos. "And look. The double axe is carved in lots of places here. Dozens. But only *some* of them have a little mark next to them. Like an arrow. I noticed it in Dad's photos last night."
She showed me. Next to the double axe on the entrance block, so small that you'd never see it unless you were looking for it, was a little scratch in the stone. A tiny arrow, pointing to the left.
§CLUE Follow the double axes. Only the ones with a tiny arrow scratched beside them.
"The Order," I said. "They marked a path."
"Nine hundred years ago," said Ela, her eyes shining. "Like breadcrumbs. Like Hansel and Gretel."
"I hope it doesn't end with a witch and an oven," said Bora.
We followed the marked axes.

Past the great staircase, which went down four floors into the hillside, with light coming in from above. Past the room of the blue dolphins, where a painting of dolphins and fish swam across the wall above a doorway, so bright and happy that you'd think it was painted yesterday. Past the storerooms, where giant clay jars as tall as Bora stood in rows, each one big enough to hide a person.
At each marked axe, there was a new tiny arrow. Left. Right. Down. Straight ahead.
Then the arrows led us through a narrow passage blocked by a rope and a sign: *NO ENTRY. AREA CLOSED.*
A guard was sitting on a stool next to the rope, in the shade, reading a newspaper.

Uncle Tarık straightened his jacket. He took his university ID card out of his wallet, walked up to the guard, and showed it to him with great dignity. "Professor Tarık Aydın, University of Istanbul," he said. "Archaeology. Very important research."
The guard looked at the card. He looked at Uncle Tarık. He looked at the three of us standing behind him, dusty and sweaty, one of us eating a cheese pie.
He shrugged, and went back to his newspaper.
We stepped over the rope.

chapters.t: Chapter Fourteen: The Throne of Griffins
p: The passage led us to the Throne Room.

It's a small, dark room, cool after the heat outside. Along the walls are stone benches. And against the middle of one wall stands a stone chair with a tall back, curved at the top like a wave. The oldest throne in Europe, Uncle Tarık whispered. Four thousand years old.

On the walls on either side of the throne were paintings of griffins: creatures with the bodies of lions and the heads of eagles, lying down in a field of red flowers, guarding the throne. Their painted eyes seemed to follow us around the room.
In front of the throne was a sunken stone basin, like a small empty pool, with steps going down into it.
"Nobody knows what it was for," said Uncle Tarık. "Some people think a queen or a priestess sat here. Some people think it was for ceremonies. Some people think it was for washing feet."
"Washing feet," said Bora. "In the oldest throne room in Europe."
"Kings have feet too," said Uncle Tarık.
The last marked double axe was carved underneath the throne itself, hidden in the shadow of the stone seat. And next to it, this time, there was no arrow.
Just a tiny compass rose. Seven points.
I knelt down and listened.

The wind here, in the cool dark of the throne room, was different from the lazy wind outside. It was slow and sleepy too, but deeper. Warmer. And it was coming from *below.* From under the floor. I could feel it on my fingertips when I put my hand flat on the stone. A gentle breath, in and out, in and out, very slow, like a giant sleeping far underground.
*Lodos is sleeping,* murmured the cool wind. *Deep, deep down. Wake him gently. He is grumpy when he wakes.*
"It's down there," I said. "The Key. Right under us."
"How do we get down there?" said Bora. "Dig?"
I put my palm flat on the double axe under the throne. I didn't know what to do. So I did what had worked before. I asked.
"Please," I said, to the stone, to the wind, to whoever was listening. "I'm a Windborn. I'm Nermin Aydın's grandson. I need to get in."
The Yıldız Key inside me woke up.

I felt it go cold in my chest, like swallowing an ice cube. The cold ran down my arm, into my hand, and out through my fingers into the stone. And frost spread across the floor in front of the throne, white and sparkling, in the shape of a perfect seven-pointed compass rose.
The throne slid sideways.
It made a grinding roar, stone on stone, so loud that I was sure the guard outside would hear. The whole room shook. Dust poured down from the ceiling. The painted griffins seemed to blink.
And where the throne had stood, a narrow stair spiraled down into the dark.
A warm breeze came up from below. It smelled of the sea, and of salt, and of very old stone.
We stood at the top of the stairs and looked down.
"Ladies first?" said Bora.
"Nice try," said Ela, and pushed him in front.

The stairs went down and down and down, deeper than any basement, deeper than the Basilica Cistern, spiraling round and round until I was dizzy. Our flashlights lit up the rough stone walls, and the steps worn into a dip in the middle by thousands of feet, a very long time ago.
Then the stairs ended, and we were in a corridor.

It was lit by glowing blue crystals set into the walls, every few meters, like little blue stars. They gave off a cold, soft light that made our faces look like ghosts. The corridor stretched away ahead of us, into the blue dark.
Then it split in three.
"Left, middle or right?" said Uncle Tarık.
"Middle," said Bora. "Middle is always safe. Like the middle seat. Or the middle of a sandwich."
We took the middle. It went for about fifty meters and split in three again.
We took the middle again. It split in three again. Then it went around a corner and ended at a blank stone wall.
"Dead end," said Ela.

We went back. We tried left. Left split into two, then three, then went around in a long curve and came back to exactly where we started. We tried right. Right led us down a ramp to a pit full of ancient bones.
Big bones. Very big bones.
"Are those," said Bora, in a very small voice, "from a cow?"

Uncle Tarık bent down and looked at them with great interest. "Hmm. Some of them are cow. Some of them, I'm not sure. This one is very interesting." He picked one up. "It's a bit like a cow, but much, much bigger. And the horns..."
"Put it DOWN, Dad," said Ela.
"Can we please go back," said Bora, "and try a different kind of adventure? A nice one? With a beach?"

"It's a real labyrinth," whispered Ela, looking around at the blue corridors. "Under the palace. The real one. The one from the story. Daedalus built it, the great inventor. He made it so complicated that even *he* almost couldn't find the way out."
"How did the hero get out?" asked Bora. "In the story. Theseus. The one who killed the Minotaur."
"The princess Ariadne gave him a ball of string," said Ela. "He tied one end at the entrance and unrolled it as he went. Then he just followed the string back."
We all looked at each other.
"Does anyone have a ball of string?" said Uncle Tarık hopefully.
Nobody had a ball of string. Ela had three paperclips, a pencil, a sharpener, a small screwdriver, a magnifying glass and an emergency chocolate bar. But no string.
"Kuzey," Ela said. "Can't the wind show us the way?"

chapters.t: Chapter Sixteen: Following the Warm Air
p: I closed my eyes.

Down here, in the labyrinth, the air was still and stuffy and old. It hadn't moved properly in thousands of years. But underneath the stillness, there was something. Very faint. A warm breeze, coming from somewhere ahead, deep in the maze. Steady and slow, like breath from a sleeping giant.
In. Out. In. Out.
"It's breathing," I said. "The Lodos. It's asleep, and it's breathing. And its breath is coming through the tunnels."
"So if we follow the warm air," said Ela slowly, "it'll lead us to the Key."
"Like Ariadne's string," I said. "But made of wind."
We went back to the place where the corridors first split. I stood at the junction, closed my eyes, and turned my face slowly from left to right, feeling the air on my cheeks.
Left: still and cool. Middle: still and cool. Right: very, very faint, a warm touch, like someone breathing on my face from far away.
"Right," I said.
It worked.

At every junction, I stopped, closed my eyes, and felt for the warm air. Left, left, right, down a ramp, right again, up three steps, through a low arch where Bora had to crawl, left, left, straight on. Bora drew a map on Ela's arm with a pen as we went, in case we needed to come back. She let him, which shows how worried she was.
Uncle Tarık kept stopping to touch the walls and saying "Incredible" and "Look at this stonework" and "This must be Bronze Age, at least," until Ela grabbed his sleeve and dragged him along.

The deeper we went, the warmer it got. The blue crystals in the walls got brighter. The breathing got louder. In. Out. In. Out. You could hear it now, not just feel it, a deep soft sound, like waves on a beach very far away.
And then, around a corner, we heard something else.
Something that wasn't breathing.
Something that was *snorting.*
A heavy, wet, angry snort, from somewhere in the dark ahead of us. Then the sound of something scraping the stone floor. Something heavy. Like a hoof.
We all stopped.
"What," whispered Bora, "was that?"
The scraping came again. Then a low, rumbling growl that I felt in my teeth.
Ela's face had gone white in the blue light. "Kuzey," she whispered. "The pit. The bones. The big ones that weren't quite a cow."
The thing in the dark snorted again. Closer.
And two eyes opened in the blackness ahead of us. Red eyes. As big as plates. Very high up off the ground.

chapters.t: Chapter Seventeen: The Bull in the Dark
p: It came out of the shadows slowly.

First the horns. Two enormous horns, curving out and up, sharp at the tips, as wide as a car. Then a head, a huge bull's head, black and shaggy, with a ring of bronze through its nose and steam pouring out of its nostrils in two hot clouds. Then a neck as thick as a tree. Then a body that was much, much worse, because it wasn't a bull's body at all.
It stood on two legs. Like a man. A giant, hairy, muscular man, three meters tall, with a bull's head, and hooves instead of feet.
The Minotaur.

It was *real.* Everything was real. Every story I had ever heard, every myth, every fairy tale. Tepegöz was real. Talos was real. The Minotaur was real, and it was standing in front of us, and it was snorting.
"Back," whispered Uncle Tarık. "Everyone back. Very slowly."
We backed away. The Minotaur followed us, one heavy step at a time. *Clop. Clop. Clop.* Its red eyes moved from Uncle Tarık to Ela to me.
Then to Bora.
And it stopped.
I got ready to blow. I could feel the North Wind gathering in my chest. But something was strange. The Minotaur wasn't charging. It was just standing there, looking at Bora, its head on one side.
And Bora was looking back at it.
"Kuzey," said Bora quietly. "Don't."
"What?"
"Don't blow it. Look at it. Look at its eyes."
I looked. The red eyes. Big and wet and red-rimmed. Not angry. Not hungry.
*Sad.*
"It's not angry," said Bora. He took a step forward. Ela grabbed his arm, but he gently pulled it free. "It's scared. And lonely. And it's been down here for... for so long. Haven't you, big guy?"
The Minotaur snorted. But it was a different snort. Softer.
"Bora," said Uncle Tarık, very calmly, in the voice of a man trying very hard not to panic. "Please step back."
Bora didn't step back. He took another step forward, very slowly, holding out his hand, palm up, the way you'd hold out your hand to a big dog you didn't know.
And in his hand, he held something. I didn't even see him take it out of his pocket.
A piece of baklava. From the airport. Slightly squashed.

"It's okay," Bora said softly. "It's okay. Nobody's going to hurt you. We're not like the others. We're not like the hero with the sword. We're just looking for something. Here. You want some? It's from Istanbul. It's really good. It's got pistachios."
The Minotaur looked at the baklava.
It looked at Bora.
It lowered its huge head, very, very slowly, until its enormous wet nose was right next to Bora's hand. It sniffed. The steam from its nostrils blew Bora's hair back.
And then, as gently as a kitten, it took the baklava from Bora's palm with its big soft lips.
It chewed. Slowly. Thoughtfully.
Then it made a sound I have never forgotten. A long, low, rumbling sound, deep in its chest, like a cello. Like a cow saying *mmmmm.*
Bora started to laugh. "Good, right? I told you!"

The Minotaur pushed its huge head against Bora's chest, almost knocking him over, like a cat asking to be stroked. And Bora, my best friend, who is afraid of the dark and heights and running out of food, put his arms as far as they would go around the neck of the Minotaur, and scratched it behind the ears.
Ela had her hand over her mouth. Uncle Tarık was taking his glasses off and putting them back on again, over and over, as if they were broken.
"Bora," I said. "How did you know?"
Bora looked up at me, his face full of wonder.

"I don't know," he said. "I just... looked at it. And I knew what it was feeling. Like it was telling me. Not in words. Just... I knew." He scratched the Minotaur under its chin, and it closed its huge red eyes in happiness. "Is that weird?"
"Yes," said Ela. "Very." But she was smiling.

chapters.t: Chapter Eighteen: The Floor of Letters
p: The Minotaur showed us the way.

It walked in front of us through the labyrinth, its hooves clopping on the stone, its horns almost scraping the walls, stopping every few steps to look back and check that Bora was still following. It never once got lost. It had lived here for longer than anyone could remember. It knew every corridor, every turn, every dead end.
"Its name," Bora announced, after a while, "is Asterion."
"How do you know that?" said Ela.
"I don't know. I just do." Bora frowned. "It's like when you know your mom is angry before she says anything. You just know."
"Asterion," said Uncle Tarık, amazed. "That's right! In some old stories, that was the Minotaur's real name! It means *star.* Like the stars on the ceiling."
"Like Yıldız," I said. "Like my Key."
The Minotaur, Asterion, looked back at me when I said that, with its big red eyes. And for a moment I felt something from it. Something like a nod.
After a long time, the corridors began to change. The walls got smoother. The blue crystals got bigger. And the warm breathing got louder and louder, until it was like being inside a giant seashell.
Then Asterion stopped.

In front of us was a big square room. The floor was covered in stone tiles, each one about the size of a pizza box, and each one carved with a letter. Not our letters. Greek letters. There were hundreds of them. On the far side of the room was a door. A huge bronze door, shaped like a bull's head, with horns curving out on either side.
Asterion snorted and backed away. It wouldn't go any further. It lay down in the corridor, with its head on its hooves, like a dog that's been told to wait.
"It's scared of the room," said Bora quietly.
"Don't step on anything," said Ela immediately.
Uncle Tarık had already stepped on something.
*Click.*

A stone spear shot out of the wall with a terrible *whoosh* and stuck quivering in the opposite wall. Exactly where Uncle Tarık's head would have been if he hadn't, at that moment, bent down to tie his shoe.
"Ah," said Uncle Tarık, very calmly, still tying his shoe. "A trap floor."
He finished tying his shoe. He stood up. He looked at the spear, still wobbling in the wall, about ten centimeters from his ear.
Then he sat down very suddenly on the floor of the corridor and said, "I think I'll just sit here for a moment."
Ela was looking at the letters. Her eyes moved fast, across and down, across and down, the way they do when she's doing a word search, which she can finish in about forty seconds.
"It's a path," she said. "It has to be. We have to spell something. A word. The right word makes a safe path to the door. Step on the wrong letter, and..." She looked at the spear. "Spears."
"What word?" said Bora.
"Something to do with the wind. With the Key. With the clue." She bit her pencil. "The warm wind sleeps. The southwest wind. Kuzey, what's the name of the god of the southwest wind? In Greek?"
"Lips," I said. "The one with the ship."

"In Greek letters it's Lambda, Iota, Psi." She scanned the floor. "There! A Lambda in the first row, look, like an upside-down V. And an Iota in the second row, right in front of it, like a straight line. And a Psi in the third row, like a trident..." She traced it with her finger in the air. "Lambda, Iota, Psi. And then again! Lambda, Iota, Psi. All the way across. Like a code."
§CLUE Only step on the letters of the southwest wind's Greek name: Λ, Ι, Ψ. Over and over.
"Are you *sure?*" said Bora.
"No," said Ela. "But I'm almost sure. Ninety percent."
"I don't love those numbers."
I took a deep breath. "I'll go first."
"Kuzey..."
"If I'm wrong, I can blow the spears away. Maybe." I stepped onto the Lambda.
Nothing happened.
I stepped onto the Iota. Nothing.
I stepped onto the Psi. Nothing.
"It works!" I called.

We hopped across the floor, one by one, landing only on the letters of the wind god's name, again and again: Λ, Ι, Ψ, Λ, Ι, Ψ. It was like the world's most dangerous game of hopscotch. I went first. Ela went second, calling out the letters. Uncle Tarık went third, holding his breath on every step. Bora went last, and landed so heavily on one Psi that the whole room shook and dust poured from the ceiling. But no spears came.
We reached the bull's-head door.
It opened by itself, with a long, low, rumbling sound, like a sigh.
And inside, something enormous began to wake up.

The room beyond the door was a huge round cave, so big that the blue crystals on the ceiling looked like stars in a night sky. The walls rose up and up into darkness. The floor was smooth and polished, like a dance floor, and it was warm under our feet. Warm air moved through the cave in long slow waves, in and out, in and out, rustling our clothes.
In the middle of the cave stood a stone altar. On the altar, glowing gold-orange like a sunset, lay a bronze needle.
The Lodos Key.

I could feel it from across the room. It was warm, like a cup of tea on a winter morning. Like a hug. Like sitting in the sun on the steps outside Grandma's building, eating a simit, on the first warm day of spring.
And sitting against the wall of the cave, with his knees pulled up and his head bowed on his arms, was a man made of bronze.

He was as tall as a four-story building. Even sitting down, his head was higher than the top of the bull's-head door. His body was smooth and shaped like a statue of an athlete, but his skin was green with age, the way old bronze goes, streaked with brown and black. Moss grew in the cracks of his giant fingers. A bird's nest sat on one of his shoulders, empty and very old.
He was so still that, for a moment, I thought he was just a statue.
Then, as we came in, his eyes opened.
Two round lights, deep in his bronze face. Orange, like hot coals in a fire.
"Visitors," said Talos.
His voice sounded like a church bell talking. It boomed and rang and echoed around the cave, and I felt it in my chest, in my bones, in my teeth.

"It has been..." He paused, as if he were counting. "Three thousand years. Three thousand years since anyone came through that door." He lifted his head slowly. Dust and pebbles rained down from his shoulders. The empty bird's nest fell and broke on the floor. "For a thousand years, I walked the shore of Crete three times every day. Round and round the whole island. I threw rocks at pirates. I protected the people. I never stopped. I never rested. I never sat down."
He looked at his huge bronze hands, as if he had never seen them before.

"And then the wise ones came. The ones with the compass rose. They brought me down here, under the palace, and they told me to guard the warm wind. So I sat down. And I have been sitting here ever since."

He began to stand. It took a long time. His joints creaked and groaned like old ship's ropes. Dust poured off him in clouds. When he was standing at last, his head almost touched the crystal stars on the ceiling.
"No one may take it," said Talos.

"Please," I said. My voice shook. I stepped forward, in front of the others. "Please, Mr. Talos. A bad man is trying to collect all seven Keys. He wants to control the weather of the whole world. He took my grandmother. We need the Lodos Key to stop him. We're from the Order. From the compass rose. My grandmother is a Keeper. I'm a Windborn."
Talos looked at me for a long moment with his burning orange eyes.

"A Windborn," he said slowly. "I have not met a Windborn in two thousand years. The last one was a girl from Persia, with a red scarf. She sang to me. I liked her." His great head tilted. "I believe you, little one. I believe you are telling the truth. I believe you are good."
"So you'll let us take it?"

"I am sorry, little one," said Talos, and his huge voice was full of sadness. "I was made to guard. I cannot choose. I have never been able to choose. I was made by the god of fire to do one thing, and I must do it, forever, whether I want to or not."
He raised his fist. It was as big as a car.
"Forgive me."
We scattered.

The fist came down where we had been standing and hit the floor so hard that the polished stone cracked like an egg, and the whole cave shook. Pieces of blue crystal fell from the ceiling and smashed around us like glass rain.
Uncle Tarık grabbed Ela and pulled her behind a pillar. Bora threw himself on the floor and rolled under the stone altar, which was a tight fit. I ran.

I ran in circles around the cave, as fast as I could, while the giant's footsteps shook the ground behind me. *BOOM. BOOM. BOOM.* Each step was like an earthquake. I could hear his joints creaking. I could hear the hot air rushing in and out of his bronze chest.
"I am sorry!" he kept booming. "I am so sorry! I do not want to!"
That was the worst part. He didn't want to hurt us. You could hear it. He was crying, I think, if bronze men can cry. But he couldn't stop.
"Ela!" I shouted, ducking under a swinging arm. "What's his weakness? In the story?"

"His ankle!" she shouted back from behind the pillar. "He had one big vein running through his whole body, from his neck to his foot, full of the gods' blood! It was closed by a bronze nail in his ankle! In the myth, the witch Medea pulled out the nail and..."
"And he ran out of life!" Bora finished from under the altar. "His ichor drained out! That's his magic blood! I saw it in a cartoon!"
I looked at the giant's feet.
On his left ankle, half hidden by moss and three thousand years of dust, was a single bronze nail. A huge one, as big as a baseball bat, sticking out of the back of his heel.
But how could we get close? Every time any of us moved, Talos turned toward us, faster than anything that big should be able to move. His burning eyes saw everything.
"Bora!" I called. "When I say go, pull the nail!"
"Why is it *always* me?" Bora's voice came from under the altar.
"Because you're the strongest!"
There was a pause.
"Fair," said Bora.
I stepped out into the open, right in front of the giant. Right in the middle of the cave. Talos turned toward me and raised both his fists.
I took the deepest breath of my whole life.

I felt the North Wind inside me, cold and wild and ready, like a wolf. And I felt the warm southwest wind sleeping in the Key on the altar, the Lodos, stirring in its sleep, listening. And all the little winds of this underground cave, the breathing air that had moved through these tunnels for thousands of years. And I asked them all for one thing.
*Dust. Please. As much as you can. Everything.*
The cave exploded.

Not with fire. With dust. Three thousand years of it, from every corner and crack and ledge. It rose up off the floor and poured down from the walls and swirled in from the tunnels in a great roaring gray cloud. It filled the air so thickly that I couldn't see my own hand in front of my face. It got in my nose, my mouth, my ears. I could hear Uncle Tarık coughing somewhere, and Ela sneezing.
Talos roared. He swung his fists blindly. One of them passed over my head so close that it blew my hair flat.
"GO!" I screamed.
I heard Bora running. Heavy footsteps, slapping on the stone. I heard the giant's foot stamp, very close to where I thought Bora was, and my heart stopped.
Then I heard a sound I will never forget.
A long, terrible screech of metal on metal. Like the world's biggest cork coming out of the world's biggest bottle.
And golden light poured out of the giant's ankle like melted honey.
The dust settled slowly.

The golden light was everywhere, flowing across the cracked floor in a shining stream, warm and bright, lighting up the whole cave like sunrise. It smelled like summer. Like honey and hot stone and thyme.
And Talos had stopped moving.

He stood very still in the middle of the cave, his fists still raised. Slowly, slowly, he lowered them. The orange glow in his eyes began to fade, the way coals fade in a fire at the end of the night. He sank down onto one knee. Then onto both knees. Then he sat back, very gently, against the wall of the cave, just the way he had been sitting when we came in. His knees up. His great hands resting on them.
He looked at me. And he smiled.
It was the strangest thing I had ever seen. A bronze face, three thousand years old, smiling. Like a statue of a king, smiling. It made him look much younger.

"Thank you," he whispered. His bell-voice was very soft now, fading, like a bell that has been rung for the last time. "Thank you, little Windborn. For three thousand years, I could not choose. I could not stop. I could not rest."
The golden light flowed out of his ankle, slower now.
"Now I am free to rest," said Talos. "That is a very good thing. Tell the girl with the red scarf, if you ever see her, that I remembered her song."
"I will," I said. I didn't know how I would ever see a girl from two thousand years ago. But I promised anyway. It seemed important.
His eyes closed.

The last of the orange light went out of them. And Talos, the bronze guardian of Crete, who had walked the shore of his island three times a day for a thousand years and then sat in the dark for three thousand more, was finally still. A statue. Peaceful. Resting.
There were moss and flowers on his bronze fingers. I didn't remember any flowers before. Little yellow ones, the color of the golden light. They had grown in a few seconds.

Bora stood beside the giant's foot, holding the enormous nail in both arms. He was covered in golden ichor from his head to his shoes, so that he looked like a statue himself, a gold one. And he was crying.
"I didn't want to hurt him," he said. His voice was shaking. "He was nice. He didn't want to fight us. I didn't want to hurt him."

"You didn't," said Ela softly. She came out from behind the pillar, covered in dust, her glasses gray with it, and put a hand on Bora's golden shoulder. "Bora. Listen to me. You didn't hurt him. You set him free. That's what he wanted. He *said* so."
Bora looked up at the giant's peaceful bronze face.
Then, very carefully, he laid the huge nail on the floor next to Talos's hand, like a present. Like flowers on a grave.
"Rest well, Mr. Talos," he said.
From the doorway behind us came a sound. A low, soft, rumbling sound, like a cello.

Asterion the Minotaur was standing in the bull's-head door, looking at the bronze giant. He had never come into this room. He had been afraid of Talos for thousands of years, I think, the way you'd be afraid of a guard who never sleeps.
Now he walked in slowly, his hooves clopping on the golden floor. He went to Talos and lowered his great horned head and touched the giant's bronze knee with his nose.
Then he turned and looked at Bora.

Bora's eyes went wide. "He says," Bora whispered, "he says the labyrinth is open now. The magic that held it closed was Talos. Now Talos is resting, so the doors are open. He can leave. He can go up, into the light. For the first time in... forever."
"Where will he go?" asked Ela.
Bora listened to something none of us could hear.

"The mountains," he said. "The White Mountains, in the west of Crete. Where nobody goes. Where there are caves, and goats, and snow on the tops, and eagles." He smiled through his tears. "He says he's always wanted to see snow."
I walked to the altar.

The Lodos Key lay there in a little hollow carved in the stone, glowing like a sunset. When I picked it up, it was warm in my hand, like a cup of tea on a winter day. And I could feel the wind inside it waking up. The warm wind of the southwest. The Lodos, the wind that blows across the Mediterranean and into Istanbul and makes the waves big and the air soft and everybody grumpy.
It stretched, and yawned, and purred like a cat.
*Mmm. Hello, Windborn,* it said sleepily. *You smell like home. Like the Bosphorus. Is it time to wake up?*
"Hello, Lodos," I said, smiling. "Yes. It's time. We're going to keep you safe."
"Actually," said a voice from the doorway, "*we* are."
Vex Vane stood in the bull's-head doorway.

Four Grays stood behind him, and his sister stood at his side. He was wearing a gray glove on each hand now, one on the left and one on the right, and cold mist curled off both of them and drifted down to the floor like smoke. Where it touched the stream of golden ichor, the ichor froze into hard yellow ice.

He must have followed us the whole way. Through the labyrinth. Following... what? The map Bora had drawn on Ela's arm? No, that was impossible. He must have had a Gray waiting at the ferry. Or a tracking spell. Or something.
It didn't matter. He was here.
Asterion the Minotaur saw him and snorted. He lowered his horns.
"Call off your cow, Windborn," said Vex, "or I'll freeze it solid." He raised one gloved hand toward Asterion. Frost shot across the floor.
"Asterion, no!" Bora shouted. "Go! Go to the mountains! Go now!"

The Minotaur looked at Bora. Then, with a long low cry like a foghorn, he turned and ran. Not toward Vex. Away, into one of the tunnels on the far side of the cave, his hooves thundering, until the sound faded into the deep.
"Smart cow," said Vex.
"Bull," said Bora. "He's a *bull.* Well, half."
