Vex ignored him. He held out his gloved hand to me. "Hand it over," he said, "and nobody else gets frozen."
He pointed his other hand at Uncle Tarık.
Ice exploded across the floor and climbed up Uncle Tarık's legs, white and crackling, gluing his feet to the stone.
"Dad!" shouted Ela.
"I'm fine!" said Uncle Tarık. "My toes are a little cold! That's all!"
I held the Key against my chest. I could feel it, warm and frightened, like a bird. "No," I said.

Vex raised his gray hands. The ice crawled up Uncle Tarık's legs. To his knees. To his waist. Uncle Tarık's face went pale. His lips started to turn blue. He was trying to smile, to show us he was fine, but his teeth were chattering.
"Your choice, Windborn," said Vex. "A needle or your uncle. I'll count to five. One."
I looked at Vera. She was staring at the floor, her fists clenched at her sides, her face white as paper. *Help us,* I thought. *Please. You helped before. Please.*
"Two."
She didn't move.
"Three."
The ice reached Uncle Tarık's chest.

I looked at him. Brave, clumsy, kind Uncle Tarık, who had flown us across the sea on his airline miles. Who had stood in front of six Grays with an umbrella. Who sat on a stair in a secret chamber and gave Bora a packet of crisps.
"Four."
There was no choice. Not really. There never had been.
"STOP!" I shouted. "Stop. Here. Take it."
I held out the Lodos Key.
Vex snatched it from my hand. It burned him through the glove. I saw him flinch, saw the pain flash across his face. But he held on, and laughed.
"One to one," he said. "Father will be so pleased."
The ice on Uncle Tarık melted all at once into a big puddle, and he sat down in it, gasping, and Ela threw her arms around him.
The Grays turned and filed out through the bull's-head door, one by one, in step. Vex followed them, tossing the Lodos Key in the air and catching it again, smiling his father's smile.
Vera went last.
At the door, she stopped. She looked back at me. Her eyes were wet. Her lips moved, without any sound, shaping two words.
*I'm sorry.*
Then she was gone.
We climbed back up through the labyrinth in silence.

It was easy now. Talos was resting, the magic was gone, and the tunnels just led up. Every corridor went in only one direction, toward the light, as if the labyrinth was tired of being a labyrinth and wanted us to leave. Bora found the place where Asterion's hoofprints went off down a side tunnel, heading west, toward the mountains. He stood looking at them for a long time.

The sun was setting over Crete when we came out from under the throne. The sky was the color of the Lodos Key: warm orange, fading to gold. The tourists had all gone home. The guard had gone. The cicadas had stopped singing. The ruins of Knossos were quiet and empty and pink in the evening light.
I sat down on a broken red column and put my head in my hands.
"I lost it," I said. "We fought a giant. We crossed a trap floor. We made friends with a *Minotaur.* And then I just gave it to him."
"You saved my dad," said Ela fiercely, sitting down next to me. Her eyes were red. "That's not losing. That's the opposite of losing."
"I would have done the same," said Bora, sitting on my other side, still sticky and golden. "Well. I would have panicked first. For a long time. Then I would have done the same."
Uncle Tarık stood in front of us. His trousers were still wet. His hair was even wilder than usual, full of dust. He looked very tired, and very old suddenly, and very kind.

"Kuzey," he said gently. "Your grandmother once told me something, years ago, when Ela was a baby. I didn't understand it then. I thought it was just one of her strange sayings. She said: 'The winds cannot be owned. They can only be borrowed.'"
I looked up at him.
"Maybe Mordecai has borrowed that Key," said Uncle Tarık. "But a wind always goes home in the end. Doesn't it?"

As if it heard him, a warm breeze blew across the ruins of Knossos. It lifted the dust. It rustled the olive trees. And inside it, so faint that I almost missed it, I heard a sleepy voice. Very far away. Getting farther away every second.
*I remember you, Windborn. I remember the way you held me. Not like him. Not like the cold hand. I will come back to you. Wait for me.*
The Lodos. Even from Vex's pocket, wherever he was, it was talking to me.
I stood up.

"It's not over," I said. "Mordecai has one Key. We have one. There are five more. And he can't find them without a Windborn. *He needs me.* That's why he let Vex follow us instead of just grabbing me. He needs me to find them."
"Which means," said Ela slowly, opening the Clue Book, "he'll keep following us. Everywhere."
"Which means," I said, "maybe one day we can lead him exactly where we want him."
Ela looked at me. Then, slowly, she grinned.
"Kuzey Aydın," she said. "Are you planning something?"
"Not yet," I admitted. "But I will."

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Four: Meanwhile, in the White Mountains
p: *This part of the story comes from a newspaper in Crete. Ela found it online, a week later, and printed it out, and glued it into the Clue Book.*
High in the White Mountains of western Crete, where the roads end and the paths begin, an old shepherd named Yiorgos lived alone with his three hundred goats in a stone hut.

He had lived there for fifty-three years. He knew every rock, every cave, every eagle's nest in those mountains. Nothing surprised him anymore. He had seen wild goats called kri-kri leap across cliffs as tall as buildings. He had seen eagles carry off lambs. He had seen snow fall in May. Once, he had seen a German tourist in sandals try to climb to the top of the highest mountain. He had to rescue him.
So when his dogs started barking at three o'clock in the morning, Yiorgos didn't worry. He took his lantern and his big walking stick and went out into the snow to see what it was.
It was a bull.

At least, at first he thought it was a bull. A huge black one, with horns as wide as a car, standing at the edge of the goat pen in the moonlight. Its breath was smoking in the cold air. It was looking up at the stars.
Then it stood up on two legs.
Yiorgos, as he told the newspaper later, "said a few words that I cannot repeat in a newspaper."

The creature looked at him. It had big red eyes. Sad eyes, Yiorgos said. Like a dog that has been left outside in the rain. Then it looked down at the snow, and it bent down, very slowly, and picked some up in its huge hairy hands. It looked at the snow for a long time, the way a child looks at a present.
Then it put the snow in its mouth, and made a sound like a cello. *Mmmmm.*
Yiorgos lowered his walking stick.
"You're hungry," he said. He didn't know why he said it. "You poor thing. Where did you come from?"
The creature looked at him with its sad red eyes.

So Yiorgos went back into his hut, and came out with a whole round of his best cheese, the one he had been saving for Christmas. He threw it into the snow. The creature picked it up, sniffed it, and ate it in two bites. Then it made the cello sound again, much louder, and the goats all started bleating at once, as if they were answering.
"You can stay," said Yiorgos, "if you don't eat my goats."
The creature shook its huge head, as if to say *I would never,* and lay down in the snow next to the goat pen, with its head on its hooves.
The newspaper printed the story on page eleven, under the title *SHEPHERD CLAIMS 'MINOTAUR' IS EATING HIS CHEESE.* Most people laughed. The newspaper called Yiorgos "a colorful local character."
But Ela glued the article into the Clue Book. And next to it, Bora drew a picture of a Minotaur in the snow, with a smile on its face and a piece of cheese in its hand.
He says it's the best drawing he's ever done.
He also says Yiorgos has, at last report, stopped losing goats to eagles. Nobody knows why. But the eagles of the White Mountains have become very, very careful.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Five: Meanwhile, on the Ferry Back
p: *Vex told Kuzey about this much later. On a rooftop in Mexico, in the middle of the night.*
The Lodos Key was screaming.
Vex sat alone on the back deck of the night ferry from Crete, in the dark, with the Key in his gloved hand, and he couldn't make it stop.
It had started the moment he grabbed it from the boy's hand in the cave. A thin, high sound. Not out loud. Inside his head. Inside his bones. Like a kettle that nobody would take off the stove.
He had thought it would be quiet. He had thought a Key would be like a trophy. Something you hold up, and everyone cheers.
It wasn't like that at all.
The Key was hot. Even through the glove, it burned. And it was *fighting* him. He could feel it, squirming in his fist, like a bird trying to get out of a cage. Twisting. Pushing. Trying to get away.
Trying to get back to the boy.
"Stop it," Vex whispered. "Stop it. Please. You're mine now. Father's. Stop."
The Key screamed louder.

He looked down at it. At the warm orange glow, flickering between his gloved fingers, like a sunset through a fence. And for one second, just one, he heard it. Not the scream. Under the scream. Words. A sleepy, warm voice, very far away.
*I remember him,* it said. *I remember the way he held me. Like a friend. Not like you. Not like the cold hand. I will go back to him. One day. I will go back.*
Vex sat very still.
Behind him, the door to the deck opened. His sister came out, in her coat, and sat down next to him on the cold bench, without saying anything.
They sat there together for a long time, watching the dark sea. The ferry's lights made a long golden road on the water behind them.
"It's crying," said Vex at last. "The Key. Can you hear it?"
Vera was quiet. Then she said, "No. But I can see your face."
Vex didn't say anything.
"Vex," said Vera. "When Father holds it. In his stone hand. Will it stop crying?"
Vex thought about the way his father's hand was cracked. The way it shook sometimes, when he thought nobody was looking.
"No," he said. "I don't think it will ever stop."
The ferry rolled on through the dark, toward Athens. And in Vex's fist, the Lodos went on screaming, all the way home.
He put his other hand over it, to try to keep it warm.
He didn't know why he did that.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Six: Meanwhile, at the Gray Tower
p: *Another part of the story that Kuzey only heard about much later.*
The fog around the gray tower was so thick that night that Vex walked into the door.

He rubbed his nose and climbed the long cold stairs, round and round, to the top of the tower, where his father was waiting in a room full of maps. Maps on the walls, maps on the floor, maps on the ceiling. And in the middle, on a table, a leather map exactly like the one Kuzey had. The same seven stars. Three of them dark now.
Mordecai Vane did not turn around when his son came in.
"Well?" he said.
Vex held out the Lodos Key.
His father turned. He looked at the glowing bronze needle in his son's gloved hand, and something flickered in his cold green eyes. Hunger. Joy. Something else.
He took off his own glove.
His stone hand was gray all the way to the wrist now. The cracks had spread since Istanbul. He picked up the Lodos Key in his bare stone fingers.
The Key screamed.

Not out loud. But Vex felt it, in his teeth, in his bones, a high shriek like a kettle boiling over. The warm golden light of the Key flickered and dimmed. Frost raced across its surface. And the Key went still and cold and dull, like an old spoon.
Mordecai closed his eyes and breathed in, slowly.
When he breathed out, the air came out warm. Warm and damp, like the Lodos wind. Outside the window, the fog swirled, and for a moment, just a moment, a warm breeze blew through the cold gray tower.
Then Mordecai coughed. A long, painful cough. And when he opened his eyes, there was a new crack in his stone hand, running from his thumb up toward his wrist.
"One to one," he said softly. "Well done, Vex."
Vex's heart leaped. His father never said *well done.*
"And your sister?" said Mordecai. "How did she help?"
Vex hesitated. He thought about Vera, standing still in the cave while he counted to five. Vera, whispering *I'm sorry* at the door.
"She helped," he lied. "She was very helpful."
His father looked at him for a long time. Then he turned back to his maps.
"Go to bed," he said.

Down the hall, in a cold little room at the top of the tower, Grandma Nermin was sitting by her window when she felt it. A warm breeze, slipping through the crack, carrying a smell of salt and summer and the Bosphorus.
The Lodos. Here. A prisoner, like her.
"Oh, my poor dear," she whispered. "Oh, you poor thing. Don't be afraid. He's coming. My Kuzey is coming. He will set you free."
The warm breeze curled around her hands for a moment, like a frightened cat.
Then it was gone. Back to the cold stone hand that held it.
The next morning, Uncle Tarık announced that we were taking a day off.

"No Keys," he said firmly, at breakfast, in our little hotel in Heraklion. "No giants. No monsters. No Grays. No clues. Today, we are going to the beach. And we are going to eat ice cream. And nobody is going to fight anybody."
"But..." said Ela.
"*Nobody,*" said Uncle Tarık, "is going to fight anybody. That is an order from the oldest person here. Even you, Ela."
Ela opened her mouth to argue. Then she closed it. I think she was tired too.
So we went to the beach.

It was a little beach on the north coast of Crete, with white sand and water so clear and blue that you could see the fish swimming around your feet. It was November, so the water was cold, but not too cold. Not for Bora. Bora ran straight into the sea, shouting, and floated on his back for an hour, looking at the sky, washing off the last of the golden ichor.
Ela sat under an umbrella, reading. Not the Clue Book. A real book. A novel, about a girl detective in London. She said it didn't count as working because it was fiction.
Uncle Tarık fell asleep on the sand with a newspaper on his face, and got sunburned in the shape of the headlines.
And I sat at the edge of the water and talked to the wind.

Not about Keys. Not about Mordecai. Just talking. The sea wind of Crete was warm and lazy and friendly, and it told me stories. About the ships that had sailed here, for thousands of years: Minoan ships with painted sails, Greek ships, Roman ships, Venetian ships, pirate ships. About the dolphins, and the octopuses in the rocks, and the old fisherman at the end of the beach who talked to the wind too, although he didn't know it could hear him.
*You did well yesterday, Windborn,* it said, after a while. *You chose your uncle over the Key. Many would not have.*
"Mordecai would have chosen the Key."
*Yes,* said the wind. *That is why we do not love him. And why we will not love him. No matter how hard he squeezes.*
I picked up a flat stone and threw it across the water. It skipped four times. With a little help from the wind, it skipped eleven.

In the afternoon, Bora called his mom. He told her about the museum, and the ferry, and the dolphins. He didn't tell her about Talos or the Minotaur. "Yes, Mom. Yes, I'm eating vegetables. Yes. There was a salad. With cheese on it. The cheese was very big."
Then he went quiet for a long time, listening, and when he hung up, he sat on the sand next to me.
"Kuzey," he said. "The Minotaur. Asterion. When I talked to him. I could really understand him. Like, really."
"I know. I saw."

"It's never happened before. I mean, I always liked animals. Dogs always come to me. Cats. Even the goat on the ferry." He frowned at the sea. "But I never *heard* them before. Not like that." He looked at me, and his face was worried. "Do you think there's something wrong with me?"
I thought about the first time the wind spoke to me, a long time ago, when I was very small. How scary it was. How I didn't tell anyone for years.
"No," I said. "I think there's something right with you."
Bora thought about that. Then he smiled, and put his arm around my shoulders, and we sat there and watched the sun go down over the sea.
It was the best day of the whole trip. I didn't know yet how much we would need it.
On the way back from the beach, Uncle Tarık stopped at a little shop in a village and bought a new umbrella.
It was the biggest umbrella in the shop. It was black, with a heavy wooden handle carved like a duck's head, and a sharp metal point at the end. When he opened it, it was as big as a small tent.
"For rain," he said, when Ela raised her eyebrows.
"It's not raining," said Ela.
"It might," said Uncle Tarık. "In Iceland."

He practiced with it all the way back to the hotel. Swinging it. Poking it. Opening it very fast, *whoomp,* in front of his face like a shield. He accidentally poked a lemon tree, a lamp post and a small dog, who was not hurt but was very offended.
"Dad," said Ela. "What are you doing?"
"Nothing," said Uncle Tarık, and he opened the umbrella in front of his face again. *Whoomp.*
That evening, I found him on the hotel roof, alone, still practicing. He was swinging the umbrella in the air in slow circles, frowning, like someone learning a dance from a video.
He stopped when he saw me, a bit embarrassed.
"I looked it up," he said. "On the internet. There's a martial art with umbrellas. From the old days in London. Gentlemen used to defend themselves with them." He swung it again. "I'm not very good."
"Uncle Tarık," I said. "You don't have to fight."

"Yes, I do." He lowered the umbrella. "Kuzey, yesterday, in that cave, I was frozen to the floor. Frozen like a fish in a freezer. And you had to give up the Key, because of me. Because I couldn't move. Because I was *useless.*"
"You weren't useless."
"I was a hostage," said Uncle Tarık. "That's the opposite of useful."
I didn't know what to say. So I went over and sat on the little wall at the edge of the roof. After a while, he sat down next to me, with his giant umbrella across his knees.
"You know who taught me what the double axe was?" I said. "And Aeolus and his bag of winds? And the Minotaur's real name? And that the Parthenon columns lean in, so they look straight?"
"Anyone could have told you those things."

"But you did," I said. "And when I couldn't find the clue at the Tower of the Winds, you're the one who could read the Greek letters. Not me. Not Ela. You. And you got us on the ferry, and you got us into Knossos past the guard, and you've used up all your airline miles, and you made probably-lasagna." I looked at him. "And you're here. My mom and dad are on the ice. Grandma's in the tower. You're the only grown-up who's here."
Uncle Tarık didn't say anything for a long time.
Then he cleared his throat and took off his glasses and cleaned them very carefully on his shirt, even though they were already clean.
"Thank you, Kuzey," he said.
"You can keep practicing with the umbrella, though," I said. "It's kind of cool."
He laughed, and stood up, and opened it with a big *whoomp.*

It caught the wind. And the wind, which I think was being mischievous, gave it a big push. And Uncle Tarık, still holding on, rose about a meter into the air, legs kicking, like Mary Poppins, before I managed to ask the wind very firmly to put him down.
He landed on his bottom on the roof.
"Well," he said, after a moment. "That was exciting, wasn't it?"
He sounded exactly like Grandma.
I woke up at three in the morning because the room was cold.

Not a little bit cold. Freezing cold. The kind of cold that gets into your bones. I could see my breath in the light from the street. And there was frost on the inside of the window, spreading slowly in feathery white patterns.
And someone was in the room.

I lay very still with my eyes half open. Two tall shapes stood by the table in the corner, where Ela had left her bag, and the Clue Book, and the leather map of the Seven Winds. Two shapes in gray suits. Their fog-gray eyes glowed very faintly in the dark, like the eyes of cats.
One of them was rolling up the map.
I sat up so fast that I banged my head on the shelf above the bed. "HEY!"
The Grays turned to look at me with their blank faces. Then they ran. Out of the door, down the stairs, the map tucked under one gray arm.
"Bora! Ela! The MAP!"
Bora sat up in bed with a snort. "Wha? Who? Is it breakfast?"

I didn't wait. I ran out of the room in my pajamas and bare feet, down the stairs, past the sleepy man at the reception desk, and out into the street. The two Grays were already at the end of the road, running toward the harbor. Not running like people. Running like machines, perfectly in step, arms swinging exactly the same.
I ran after them. Behind me, I heard Bora and Ela clattering down the stairs, and Ela shouting, "Kuzey, wait! Your SHOES!"

The streets of Heraklion were dark and empty. My bare feet slapped on the cold stones. The Grays turned onto the long harbor wall that runs out into the sea, toward the Venetian fortress at the end of it.

The fortress is called the Koules. It's a big square castle, built five hundred years ago by the Venetians, who ruled Crete back then. It sits at the very end of the harbor wall, with the sea on three sides, and a carved stone lion with wings on its wall, the symbol of Venice. At night, it's lit up gold.
The Grays ran straight toward it. And at the end of the wall, waiting in the shadow of the fortress, was a small boat with its engine running.
If they got on the boat, the map was gone.
"Wind!" I gasped. I was running so hard I could barely speak. "Please... help... the boat..."
The sea wind of Crete was asleep. It was three in the morning. It mumbled something and rolled over.
I stopped running. I stood on the harbor wall, in my pajamas, with my lungs burning, and I closed my eyes.
And I didn't ask the sea wind. I asked my own wind. The one inside me.
*Yıldız,* I said. *North Wind. Are you there?*
It woke up instantly. It had never been asleep. It was cold and fierce and *mine,* and it had been waiting for me to ask.
*Always, Windborn. What do you need?*
"Ice," I said. "Please. On the wall. In front of them."
I breathed out.

A stream of frost shot out of my mouth and raced along the harbor wall like a white snake, faster than the running Grays, passing them, and spreading out across the stones in front of them in a long sheet of smooth, slippery ice.
The Grays hit the ice running.

Their feet went out from under them. Both of them. At exactly the same time, perfectly in step, the way they did everything. They slid along the ice on their backs, spinning slowly, like two gray teabags on a kitchen floor, all the way to the end of the wall, and *splash, splash,* right into the harbor.
The map flew up into the air.
I watched it spin, up and up, against the gold light of the fortress. It started to fall. Toward the water.
And a hand reached out from the shadow of the fortress and caught it.
A small hand. A girl's hand.

Vera Vane stepped out of the shadows, holding the rolled-up map. She was wearing a black jacket with the hood up. Behind her, the boat's engine was still running, and a Gray was at the wheel, waiting.
We looked at each other across the ice. She was about ten meters away. Down in the water, the two Grays were splashing and trying to climb the wall.
"Give it back," I said. "Please."
She looked at the map in her hand for a long moment.
"My father says you need it to find the Keys," she said quietly. "He says if we take it, you'll be lost. And you'll have to come to him. And ask for help."
"Is that what you want?"
Vera didn't answer. She looked at the boat. She looked at the Grays in the water. She looked at me, standing barefoot on the harbor wall in my pajamas, with frost on my eyebrows.
Then she bent down, put the map on the ground, and slid it across the ice toward me. It spun across the frozen stones and stopped right at my feet.
"I dropped it," she said. "In the fight. It fell. I couldn't reach it. That's what happened. Okay?"
"Okay," I said.
She turned and jumped into the boat. The Gray at the wheel didn't seem to have noticed anything. The boat roared away into the dark, leaving the two wet Grays still splashing in the harbor.
I picked up the map. My hands were shaking.
Ela and Bora came running up behind me, Ela holding my shoes, Bora in his pajamas with a hotel blanket around his shoulders like a cape.
"Did you get it?" panted Ela. "Did you get the map?"
I held it up.
"How?" said Bora. "What happened?"
I looked out at the dark sea, where the boat's light was getting smaller and smaller.
"Someone dropped it," I said.

chapters.t: Chapter Thirty: The Message in the Ice
p: The next evening, in our little hotel in Heraklion, I spread out the leather map of the Seven Winds on the bed.
Istanbul's star had gone dark. That Key was found. And the star over Greece had gone dark too, on Crete, the moment I picked up the Lodos Key. Even though Vex had taken it, the star stayed dark.
"So the stars don't show who *has* the Keys," said Ela, writing in the Clue Book. "Just which Keys have been found. Two found. Five to go."
But far to the north, on an island at the very top of the map, near the edge of the world, a new star was glowing. Brighter every minute. Brighter than it had been yesterday. As if it was waking up.
"Iceland," whispered Ela.
"The land of fire and ice," said Uncle Tarık, looking over our shoulders. "Volcanoes and glaciers. Geysers. Vikings. And trolls, if you believe the old stories."
"I'm starting to believe all the old stories," said Bora.

Uncle Tarık was already on his laptop, looking at flights. "If we go through Athens and then London," he muttered, "and then Reykjavik... I have enough miles... but only just... and we'll have to sit next to the toilets again..."
"Iceland is cold, right?" said Bora. "Really cold?"
"In November? Very cold," said Ela. "Snow. Ice. Storms. Only about six hours of daylight a day."
"Six hours?" said Bora, horrified. "What do they do the rest of the time? Do they eat?"
That was when the window frosted over.

It happened with a sudden crackle, like someone stepping on thin ice. One second, the window was clear, showing the lights of the harbor and the dark sea. The next, it was white. Covered in frost. Thick and feathery and cold.
The room went very cold. Our breath came out in clouds.
And letters appeared in the ice. Slowly. One at a time. Written by an invisible gray finger, scratching through the frost, squeak, squeak, squeak.
*ONE TO ONE, LITTLE WINDBORN.*
*SEE YOU IN THE COLD.*
We stared at it. Nobody moved.
Then the frost melted, all at once, and ran down the glass like tears, and the window was clear again. Just the harbor. Just the sea.
Bora looked at the window. Then at me.
"I," he said, "am going to need a much bigger coat."

We bought coats the next morning, in a shop in Heraklion that sold coats to tourists who were going skiing in the mountains. Bora's was bright orange and so puffy that he looked like a giant pumpkin. Ela's was dark blue, with lots of pockets, which she said was "very practical for clues." Uncle Tarık bought the cheapest one in the shop, which was purple, with a fur hood. I bought a red one.
And I wrapped Grandma's blue scarf around my neck, over the top.

At the airport, waiting for our plane, I went to the big window and looked out at the runway. Planes were taking off into a perfect blue sky. Somewhere out there, far to the north, past the mountains and the seas and the whole of Europe, was an island of fire and ice.
And somewhere, in a gray tower by a gray sea, my grandmother was sitting by a window, singing. And the Lodos was in a stone hand, cold and frightened.
"I'm coming," I told the wind. "Tell her I'm coming. Tell the Lodos too."
*We will tell them,* said the wind of Crete. *Go north, little Windborn. Your own wind is waiting for you there. The north is strong in Iceland. You will be stronger there too.*
Ela came and stood next to me. She had the Clue Book under her arm.
"I wrote a new page," she said. "Want to see?"
She opened it. At the top, in her small neat writing, it said:
*SCORE*
*Kuzey: 1 (Yıldız)*
*Mordecai: 1 (Lodos)*
*Keys left: 5*
*Friends made: Rıza Usta, Cousin Nikos, Asterion the Minotaur, Kyria Despina, Mehmet Abi, the winds of Athens, Talos (sort of)*
*Friends Mordecai made: 0*
I laughed. "That last one isn't a real score."
"It's the most real score," said Ela seriously. "That's the one that matters. Grandma's letter said so. 'You have something he will never have.'"
The plane was boarding. Bora was waving at us from the gate, in his huge orange coat, holding a bag of Cretan honey cakes "for the journey."
I took one last look at the blue sky of Greece. Then I turned and walked toward the plane, and toward the north, and toward the cold.

For hundreds of years, sailors on the Black Sea, the Bosphorus and the Mediterranean used a wind rose to name the winds. Each wind had its own name and its own personality, and every sailor knew them by heart. These are the seven winds of the Order of the Compass Rose.
**Yıldız (North).** Named after the North Star, *yıldız* means "star." A cold, clear, starry wind. Kuzey's own wind.
**Poyraz (Northeast).** The great wind of the Black Sea. When the Poyraz blows hard, the fishermen go home and the ferries rock.
**Gündoğusu (East).** "Sunrise." The wind that comes from where the sun is born each morning.
**Keşişleme (Southeast).** Named after the monks, the *keşiş,* who lived on the mountains to the southeast. A warm, dry wind from the deserts.
**Kıble (South).** The wind from the direction of Mecca. Hot, and full of sand.
**Lodos (Southwest).** A warm, wild, wet wind that brings big waves and headaches. People in Istanbul say the Lodos makes everyone grumpy.
**Karayel (Northwest).** "Black wind." A stormy, dark wind that brings clouds and sudden rain.
And the eighth, the west wind, the **Batı**, the one that would not make a deal? Nobody knows. It is still wild. That is another story.

chapters.t: The Real Places in This Book
p: **The Tower of the Winds.** A real eight-sided marble tower in the Roman Agora in Athens, built about 2,000 years ago by an astronomer named Andronikos. It was a clock, a weather vane and a calendar. Each side has a carved flying wind god, and there are sundials underneath. Lips, the southwest wind, really is holding the back of a ship.

**The Parthenon.** The great temple of Athena on the Acropolis, about 2,500 years old. Its columns really do lean in slightly, and bulge a tiny bit in the middle, so that from far away they look perfectly straight.
**Aeolus and the bag of winds.** From the *Odyssey,* one of the oldest stories in the world. The sailors really did open the bag, and the winds really did blow them all the way back home.
**Plaka.** The oldest neighborhood in Athens, under the Acropolis, full of narrow streets, flowers and cats.

**Knossos.** The palace of the Minoans on Crete, nearly 4,000 years old. It has a throne room with painted griffins, a room with painted dolphins, red columns that get thinner at the bottom, and a very confusing layout, which may be why later Greeks told stories about a labyrinth. The double axe, the labrys, is carved in many places.
**The bull-leaping painting.** It's real, and you can see it in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum, along with the snake goddesses and the golden double axes.

**Talos and the Minotaur.** Both are from Greek myths. In the stories, Talos was a bronze giant who walked around Crete three times a day, and he was defeated when someone pulled out the nail in his ankle. Some old stories really do say the Minotaur's name was Asterion, which means *star.*
**The White Mountains.** Real mountains in western Crete, with snow on top in winter, and wild goats called kri-kri that leap across the cliffs.
*Here is the first chapter of the next book,* The Black Wind's Rune.
**Chapter One: The Coldest Place I've Ever Been**
I am the North Wind's favorite person, and I was still freezing.

Iceland at the end of November is dark for most of the day. When we landed at Keflavík airport at eleven in the morning, it looked like midnight. Snow blew sideways across the runway, and the wind howled so hard that the plane wobbled like a jelly on a plate. Three people screamed. Bora said a prayer. I said "please, please, please" to the wind under my breath, and it said *oh, all right,* and the plane landed with a bump.

The Icelandic wind was nothing like the chatty old men of Athens or the lazy cat-wind of Crete. It was huge and slow and wild, and it spoke in deep, rumbling words, very far apart, like a giant talking in its sleep.
*Windborn,* it rumbled. *Long. Have you. Been coming.*
"Hello," I said politely, through the window of the plane.
*The Black Wind,* it rumbled. *Waits. In the ice.*
And then it said nothing else at all for an hour.

"The Black Wind," I told the others in the rental car, while Uncle Tarık tried to remember which side of the road to drive on. (In Iceland it's the right side, like Turkey, so I don't know why he was confused. He said it was "the general atmosphere.") "That's the Karayel. The northwest wind."

"Kara means black," said Ela, writing in the Clue Book. "In the old Turkish wind rose, the northwest wind is called the black wind because it brings dark storms. Sudden ones. The fishermen are scared of it."

Bora was wearing his huge orange coat, plus a second coat he had borrowed from Uncle Tarık underneath it, plus two hats, plus a scarf his grandmother had knitted that went around his neck five times, plus mittens shaped like bears. Only his eyes were visible, peeking out between the scarf and the hats.
"I can't feel my face," he said. "Is my face still there?"
"Probably," said Ela.
We drove out of the airport into a landscape that looked like another planet.

Black lava fields, stretching away forever, covered in green moss and snow, lumpy and strange, like a giant had spilled chocolate pudding and then it froze. Steam rising out of cracks in the ground, as if the earth was breathing. Mountains like sleeping animals, white and gray and black. No trees at all. Not one. Ela said the Vikings cut them all down a thousand years ago and they never grew back.

And in the dark sky, when the clouds tore open for a moment, there was green light. Swirling like ribbons. Ripples of green and purple, moving slowly across the stars, like curtains blowing in a window.
"The northern lights," whispered Uncle Tarık, and nearly drove into a sheep.
The sheep looked at us with great contempt and walked slowly across the road.
I stared up at the lights. They were the most beautiful thing I had ever seen. They moved like they were alive. Like they were dancing to music I couldn't hear.
And for a second, I could have sworn the lights moved into the shape of a face.
A thin face. With too many teeth.
Then the clouds closed, and it was gone.
I didn't say anything. But I pulled Grandma's scarf up over my nose, and I didn't look at the sky again for the rest of the drive.
§END To be continued in* The Black Wind's Rune...
